newsitem.title: USA: Republicans should do own budget -- U.S. Sen Lott.
newsitem.headline: Republicans should do own budget -- U.S. Sen Lott.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Wednesday his Republican party should draw up its own plan to balance the budget, possibly working with conservative Democrats.

"I no longer think we can afford to delay our own actions and our own preparations in producing a budget in expectation that something will happen with the administration," the Mississippi Republican said at his regular news conference.
President Clinton, however, is to meet later Wednesday with House and Senate budget committee chairmen after seeing what he called signs of budget flexibility in Congress.

Lott said he would still like to see a reduction in the Consumer Price Index, which is used to calculate the cost of living increase for government benefits, tax rate brackets and wages. But he said he would not raise the issue again.

Administration and Democratic opposition to the CPI change was so formidable that Democrats would have to make the next move if it were to occur, he said. "That phase of effort is over," he told reporters.

Lott noted that many of his Republican colleagues were upset that he had attempted to jump start the CPI change last week with the suggestion that an expert commission be set up to figure out an accurate rate. The commission chaired by Stanford economist Michael Boskin had reported earlier that it was overstated by about 1.1 percentage point per year.

"They can see full well that (House Minority Leader) Dick Gephardt and his allies in the union movement would be ginning up television spots blasting people on the change in the CPI," he said. "What we should do is what accurate, what's honest, if it needs to be raised or lowered either way."

Lott said it was possible to craft a five-year balanced budget agreement without a CPI change. "It is possible, but it makes it much more difficult." Without agreement on economic assumptions, a CPI change and greater entitlement savings, "It gets to be a long leap," to a balanced budget.

Later, Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said it was unlikely that the CPI would be considered as part of early negotiations and would probably not come up during Wednesday afternoon's budget talks between congressional leaders and the president.
